archival_memory.research_experience: I've been involved in undergrad research since my sophomore year, which has been an eye-opening experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world. I initially didn't see myself going down the research route, but a professor noticed my skills in bridging technical coding with user experience and offered me a research assistant position in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was hesitant at first, but it turned out to be a great decision.

archival_memory.research_lab_description: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. We deal with datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. My main task is working on front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards using advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering if needed.

archival_memory.first_research_project: My first research project involved visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. The raw data was enormous, consisting of daily temperature readings from buoys across the Pacific. I wrote scripts to clean and unify the data, built a pipeline for near real-time updates, and designed interfaces for researchers to explore specific regions or timeframes. I co-authored a paper on this system, which was a surreal and proud moment for me.

archival_memory.current_research_focus: I'm currently working on immersive analytics platforms, exploring how VR or AR technologies can enhance scientists' understanding of complex data. It's a leap from traditional data visualization methods, allowing users to interact with 3D representations in a virtual environment. The process involves experimentation, integrating VR headsets, and optimizing data streaming into 3D environments using engines like Unity or Unreal. It's a cutting-edge field, and every day, I'm forging my own path as there isn't a well-established best-practice library for VR data visualization yet.

archival_memory.research_life: Research life is not just about coding away in a quiet corner. It's a lot of reading, especially when trying to solve complex problems like rendering volumetric data in VR. I need to comb through conference proceedings and workshops to see if someone has already tried something similar. It can be overwhelming, but over time, I've learned to skim effectively by looking at the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. When I discover something interesting, I share it with the lab and we discuss how to incorporate that technique into our workflow.

archival_memory.interactions_with_grad_students: I have the opportunity to interact with graduate students in the lab, which can be intimidating at first due to their deep knowledge in niche fields. However, it's also inspiring to see their passion and dedication. One PhD student is developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets, aiming to integrate it with our VR platform. This concept is both wild and practical, as it can enhance real-time performance by using compressed representations. Working alongside him allows me to witness the application of advanced theoretical concepts. Spontaneous brainstorming sessions, like those in the lab break room, often lead to valuable insights and innovative ideas.

archival_memory.poster_presentations: I've had the opportunity to present posters at smaller symposiums around campus, which was a great experience. It requires boiling down complex research into easy-to-digest visuals and talking points. Initially, I was nervous about presenting to random professors or industry folks who might ask tough questions. However, the experience turned out to be more like a friendly dialogue, with people genuinely interested in what I was doing. I even met a few folks from local startups who shared interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries like marketing analytics or architecture. It opened my eyes to the potential for research to transition from academia to real-world applications.

archival_memory.publications: I've been fortunate enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and am currently working on a larger conference submission for the IEEE Visualization Conference. Our research focuses on comparing traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment in a user study. We hypothesize that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster. We've conducted user trials with 15 participants, recorded their times, and gathered UX questionnaires. Now, we're analyzing the data to determine if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a collaborative effort, with different team members handling different sections. It's a balancing act, especially with senior coursework and a capstone project to manage.

archival_memory.frustrations_of_research: Research can be frustrating at times. You may spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or discover that your idea has already been done and improved upon by others. It can feel like a punch in the gut. However, the key is to adapt. By reading existing papers, incorporating their findings, and finding new angles or applications, you can push the boundaries of research. It's a collaborative process, both within your lab and among the global research community. The sense of collaboration is truly special.

archival_memory.server_crash_story: A few months ago, one of our massive servers crashed, and we lost vital data that wasn't fully backed up. It was a frantic night of email chains and Zoom calls with the lab manager as everyone scrambled to see if we could recover the data. We managed to restore most of it, but the crisis highlighted the importance of data backups. After that, we set up a better backup system and implemented checks to ensure we don't rely on a single point of failure again. It was stressful, but also a bonding experience for the whole lab.

archival_memory.project_teammate: She's actually in my advanced algorithms class. We ended up on the same team for a project about a month ago, and that's when I really got to know her. Typically, group projects can be stressful—trying to coordinate schedules, dividing up tasks, and making sure the final product is cohesive. But in our case, it gave me a real excuse to chat with her and just understand how she thinks. The more we worked on that project, the more I realized how funny and brilliant she is. We'd be in those group Zoom calls, and while everyone else was kind of stressed about the complexity of the code, she would be cracking witty jokes about it. It's so refreshing to find someone who doesn't get overtly frazzled by the academic pressure and instead keeps the mood light. And her sense of humor is totally up my alley—dry, a bit sarcastic, but never mean-spirited.

archival_memory.project_collaboration: She's also super dedicated to her studies. I learned she's minoring in mathematics and has a real passion for discrete structures. Meanwhile, I'm more of a software-oriented person—my interests align more with system design, maybe some user interface stuff, and I dabble in data science. So our strengths complement each other pretty well. In fact, I think we worked so well together because if I got stuck on a complex analysis or a combinatorial proof, she'd walk me through it step by step. It's kind of rare in group settings that I trust another person's process so readily, but with her, it's like I know she's got it covered. We ended up getting an A on that project, but to be honest, I was just happy for the chance to collaborate with her.
archival_memory.time_management: The tricky part is figuring out if she's interested in me beyond just a team partner or a classmate. I'm so busy with everything else—applications for full-time jobs, my internship from last summer wanting me to come back after graduation, and then there are all my extracurriculars. I'm in the Robotics Club, which meets twice a week, and I'm also still involved in the sailing club. You know, I've been into sailing since I was a kid, so it's something I can't quite give up even when the semester is insane. Then there's the gym—remember, I try to work out every morning just to keep my sanity. The point is, I feel like I barely have enough hours in the day to keep up with all the responsibilities I already have. But when you really like someone, you can't help but want to carve out time for them, right?

I suppose I could just casually say I need a break from coding or something along those lines—something that doesn't feel too forced. But I don't want to overthink it, which, let's be real, is exactly what I do. I'm going to see if she has a gap on Tuesday or Thursday since my schedule is a bit more flexible those days. I keep telling myself: worst case scenario, she says she's busy, and we try another day. Or maybe she just sees me as another CS Archie. But that's life—sometimes you have to take a risk.

archival_memory.surreal_feeling: It feels a little surreal talking about crushes at this stage in college. We're all busy, we're all stressed, but at the same time, it's also a time when you can meet some of the most interesting people ever. And I feel like I've found someone I'd really like to get closer to. So yeah, that's where I'm at. I'll probably wait until after our next group meeting so I don't catch her off guard. Maybe I'll crack a small joke about how we survived advanced algorithms together, and now it's time to celebrate with a latte. Even if she says no, at least I will have tried. But something tells me she might just say yes.
